# Education in Finland: Summary
Education in Finland is built on a comprehensive, inclusive system rooted historically in Lutheran values emphasizing literacy. The compulsory comprehensive school covers nine years (grades 1–9), typically divided into primary (alakoulu, grades 1–6) and middle school (yläkoulu, grades 7–9), with instruction mainly funded and administered by municipalities. Private schools exist but must admit all students without tuition fees or selective admissions. Classes are small (usually under 20 students), and students learn two additional languages beyond their mother tongue, fostering a relaxed, play-based early education system with strong cooperation between families and society. Formal numerical grading begins locally after initial verbal assessments, with grades ranging from 4 (fail) to 10 (excellent). Social supports include free school lunches, health care, materials, and trips.
Upper secondary education, now compulsory up to age 18 since 2021, lasts three to four years and is divided into academic (lukio) and vocational tracks. Academic students take a national matriculation exam, important for university admissions, while vocational graduates receive a vocational certificate and may still pursue higher education. Advanced curricula in subjects like mathematics and languages allow tailored difficulty levels. Teachers at all levels must hold master’s degrees, reflecting the profession's high respect and selective university admission. Finnish tertiary education includes traditional research universities and universities of applied sciences. Admissions are transparent and merit-based, relying on GPA, matriculation exam results, and entrance tests without subjective factors. Tuition is free for EU/EEA students; non-EEA students pay fees. Adult and open university programs support lifelong learning and requalification.
